metadata.title: Only Four of the Nine.
metadata.subtitle: The Hook Development Skill (Prompt-Based Hooks)
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does the recommended hook type work on every lifecycle event you attach it to, or only some? Lands the carry-out that Prompt-Based hooks only fire on four of the nine events, and a hook placed on one of the other five silently never runs.

beats.narration_text: Obvious guess: the type Anthropic recommends — Prompt-Based — fires on every event you attach it to. Wrong branch. It only fires on four of the nine. So the real question is: does a Prompt-Based hook fire on only four of the nine events I use?

beats.narration_text: Two hook types, two places to put them. Prompt-Based is the recommended type — it hands Claude a bit of context and lets Claude decide what to do; the matcher names the tools it applies to, the prompt field tells Claude how to respond, thirty-second default timeout. They optimized for flexibility, at the cost of determinism. Command hooks go the other way: run a bash script, read the exit code. Zero is success — stdout goes into the transcript. Two is block — Claude sees the stderr message and stops. Any other code is non-blocking. Sixty-second default. Auditability at the cost of writing bash. One rule for portability: always use the CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT environment variable in the command path, never a hardcoded absolute one — otherwise the hook only works on the machine that authored it. And the two config formats aren't interchangeable either. Plugin hooks.json wraps everything under a description and a hooks key; the settings file skips that wrapper, and event names sit right at the top level. That split reveals who each format is for — the plugin author packaging something to distribute, or the user editing their own settings.

Nine lifecycle events exist. PreToolUse fires before a tool call, Stop when Claude's about to finish, SubagentStop for subagents, UserPromptSubmit when you send a message. Those four support Prompt-Based — the pattern is that Claude has room to reason at that moment, so handing it context makes sense. The other five — PostToolUse, SessionStart, SessionEnd, PreCompact, and Notification — are Command-only, because by then the decision either can't wait or Claude's already moved on. Four execution rules govern the rest, and each one is a design choice with a cost. One: all matching hooks run in parallel — no ordering, no cross-talk. Simpler mental model, at the price of pipelines. Two: hooks load once, at session start — no hot-swap, so you restart Claude after editing hooks.json. Consistency-within-session, at the price of ergonomics. Three: matchers are case-sensitive — Write is not write. Predictable, at the price of a class of silent misses. Four, security: quote every bash variable, validate inputs, deny path traversal and access to files like dot-env and private keys. The assumption is that bash on your machine is the attack surface, so treat it like one.

Here's the catch, and it's the whole point. Prompt-Based is the type the skill recommends — but it only fires on those same four events: PreToolUse, Stop, SubagentStop, and UserPromptSubmit. Add a Prompt-Based hook to PostToolUse expecting Claude to review a tool's output after the fact, and nothing happens. No error. No warning. The hook just never runs. That's a design choice: the loader doesn't cross-check event against hook type, so a mismatched pair fails silently instead of loudly. If a hook needs to catch something after the tool call, that has to be a Command hook.
Prompt-Based is the recommended hook type — but it only fires on four of the nine lifecycle events. Put one on PostToolUse and it silently never runs.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Write me a Claude plugin with two hooks — one that logs every Write tool call to a JSON file, and one that blocks any Write to a dot-env file. Before you write the code, walk me through it. Which hook type does each need — Prompt-Based or Command — given that logging happens after the write, on PostToolUse, and blocking happens before, on PreToolUse? Does the command path use the CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT environment variable or a hardcoded absolute path? Does the config go in the plugin hooks.json wrapper format — description and hooks key — or the flat settings format? And after editing hooks.json, what do I need to do before the hook takes effect? Show your reasoning at each step. Go deeper: ask the same model to write a Prompt-Based hook meant to review every tool's output after the fact — then, in its own words, explain why the hook it just wrote will never fire, and name the one change that would make it work.
